title: Particle Accelerators
short_intro: Particle accelerators are devices that use electromagnetic fields to propel charged elementary particles or ions to high speeds and energies. They are fundamental instruments in nuclear and particle physics for probing the microscopic structure of matter.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic working principles of linear accelerators and cyclotrons, cyclotron frequency, resonance condition, and maximum kinetic energy of accelerated ions.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Phase stability in synchrotrons, relativistic mass corrections in high-energy accelerators, betatron condition, and focusing principles like strong focusing (alternating-gradient).

prerequisites: Lorentz force on a moving charge in electric and magnetic fields
Motion of charged particles in uniform magnetic fields (circular trajectory)
Radio-frequency alternating voltage circuits and resonance

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Particle Accelerators
bullets: Accelerators are broadly classified into electrostatic (e.g., Van de Graaff generator, Cockcroft-Walton) and electrodynamic or time-dependent accelerators.
Electrodynamic accelerators use time-varying electric fields and are further subdivided into linear accelerators (Linacs) and cyclic accelerators.
Cyclic accelerators include the cyclotron, synchrotron, microtron, and betatron, designed to achieve higher energies within a constrained laboratory space.

concept_notes.heading: Working Principle of a Cyclotron
bullets: A cyclotron uses a constant magnetic field to bend charged particles into circular paths and a high-frequency alternating electric field across a narrow gap between two D-shaped hollow electrodes (dees) to accelerate them.
The time taken by a particle to complete a semi-circular path inside a dee is independent of its speed and radius, provided its mass remains constant (non-relativistic regime).
Resonance condition requires the frequency of the alternating electric field to exactly match the cyclotron frequency of the circulating ions.

concept_notes.heading: Limitations of the Cyclotron
bullets: At high energies, particles approach the speed of light, causing relativistic mass increase according to Einstein's theory.
Due to the relativistic mass increase, the revolution frequency of particles decreases, causing them to fall out of phase with the alternating electric field.
Electrons cannot be effectively accelerated in a standard cyclotron because their small rest mass causes them to become relativistic at very low kinetic energies.

concept_notes.heading: Synchrotrons and Phase Stability
bullets: A synchrotron is a cyclic accelerator in which both the magnetic field and the radio frequency are synchronized with the increasing momentum of the accelerated particle beam.
The principle of phase stability ensures that particles slightly deviating in energy or phase from the synchronous particle are automatically focused back toward the stable synchronous condition.
Synchrotrons overcome the relativistic limitations of cyclotrons, enabling the attainment of ultra-high multi-GeV and TeV energy regimes.

derivations.title: Cyclotron Frequency and Maximum Kinetic Energy
derivations.conditions: Non-relativistic charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity
steps: Equate the magnetic Lorentz force to the centripetal force: qvB = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}
Express the angular frequency or cyclotron frequency: omega = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{qB}{m}
Express the orbital frequency: f = \frac{omega}{2pi} = \frac{qB}{2pi m}
Substitute the maximum radius R of the dees to find maximum velocity v_{max} = \frac{qBR}{m}

derivations.title: Betatron Condition for Magnetic Induction Acceleration
derivations.conditions: Electrons accelerated by a changing magnetic flux in an axisymmetric magnetic field
steps: The induced electromotive force around an orbit of radius r is given by Faraday's law of induction: xi = -\frac{dPhi}{dt} = - pi r^{2} \frac{dB_{av}}{dt}, where B_{av} is the average magnetic field enclosed by the orbit.
The rate of change of momentum p = erB is balanced by the force due to the induced electric field: \frac{dp}{dt} = e E = \frac{exi}{2pi r}.
Substitute xi to get: \frac{d(erB)}{dt} = \frac{e}{2pi r} (pi r^{2} \frac{dB_{av}}{dt}) = \frac{er}{2} \frac{dB_{av}}{dt}.
For a constant orbit radius r, differentiating gives: \frac{dB}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{dB_{av}}{dt}.
Integrate to obtain the 2:1 rule: B = \frac{1}{2} B_{av}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Radius vs. Energy in a Cyclotron
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve showing particle kinetic energy increasing quadratically with the orbital radius r inside the dees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As the particle gains energy at each gap crossing, its velocity increases, and the radius of its circular trajectory expands proportionally until it reaches the maximum dee radius R.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual MCQs regarding the scaling of maximum energy with magnetic field and dee radius.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Resonance Curve of Cyclotron Oscillator
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A sharp resonance peak plotting ion current output against the frequency of the applied oscillator electric field.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Maximum energy extraction occurs strictly when the oscillator frequency matches the cyclotron frequency of the ions. Any mismatch causes phase slippage and loss of beam current.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluates understanding of resonance conditions in electrodynamic accelerators.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phase Stability Region (Bucket) in Synchrotron
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Closed separatrix curves in the phase-energy (phi-E) plane representing stable particle motion.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Particles residing within the separatrix (RF bucket) oscillate stably in phase and energy around the synchronous particle, preventing beam dispersal.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT question on longitudinal beam dynamics and phase stability.

solved_numericals.question: A cyclotron has a magnetic field of 1.5 T and a dee radius of 0.5 m. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of protons accelerated by it. (Mass of proton = 1.67 x 10^{-27} kg, charge = 1.6 x 10^{-19} C)
solution_steps: Identify given values: B = 1.5 T, R = 0.5 m, q = 1.6 x 10^{-19} C, m = 1.67 x 10^{-27} kg.
Use the formula for maximum kinetic energy: K_{max} = \frac{q^{2}B^{2}R^{2}}{2m}
Compute final energy in Joules and convert to MeV: K_{max} = 4.31 \times 10^{-12} J = \frac{4.31 \times 10^{-12}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13}} MeV approx 26.9 MeV

solved_numericals.question: In a cyclotron, deuterons are to be accelerated. The magnetic field is 1.0 T. What should be the frequency of the radio-frequency electric field? (Mass of deuteron = 3.34 x 10^{-27} kg, charge = 1.6 x 10^{-19} C)
solution_steps: Identify parameters: q = 1.6 x 10^{-19} C, B = 1.0 T, m = 3.34 x 10^{-27} kg.
Use cyclotron frequency formula: f = \frac{qB}{2pi m}

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the cyclotron frequency for an electron in a magnetic field of 0.5 T, taking relativistic effects into consideration when its kinetic energy is equal to its rest mass energy (m_{0}c^{2} = 0.511 MeV).
solution_steps: Given K = m_{0}c^{2}, total energy E = K + m_{0}c^{2} = 2 m_{0}c^{2}.
Use relativistic cyclotron frequency formula: f = \frac{qB}{2pi gamma m_{0}}

assumptions_and_limitations: Cyclotrons assume constant particle mass, which fails at relativistic speeds (v approaching c).
Magnetic field uniformity across the dee region is assumed to maintain constant orbital frequency in simple cyclotrons.
Energy losses due to synchrotron radiation are neglected in non-relativistic circular accelerators but become dominant for ultra-relativistic electrons in circular rings.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A cyclotron can accelerate electrons to very high relativistic energies just like protons.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electrons cannot be accelerated efficiently in a standard cyclotron.
common_misconceptions.why: Due to their extremely small rest mass, electrons reach relativistic speeds at very low kinetic energies, causing them to lose resonance with the fixed oscillator frequency.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The electric field inside the dees of a cyclotron accelerates the charged particles continuously.
common_misconceptions.correct: The electric field is zero inside the hollow dees and acceleration occurs only across the narrow gap between them.
common_misconceptions.why: Dees act as Faraday cages shielding the interior from external electric fields; particles only gain energy when crossing the gap.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Increasing the radio-frequency voltage in a cyclotron increases the maximum final energy of the particles.
common_misconceptions.correct: The maximum kinetic energy depends only on the magnetic field B and the outer radius R of the dees.
common_misconceptions.why: Higher RF voltage increases the rate of energy gain and reduces the number of turns needed, but the maximum orbit radius is capped by the physical dimensions of the dees.

quick_revision: Cyclotron frequency depends directly on magnetic field and charge-to-mass ratio, and is independent of radius and velocity in the non-relativistic domain.
Maximum kinetic energy in a cyclotron is proportional to B^{2}R^{2}.
Synchrotrons dynamically adjust both magnetic field and RF frequency to maintain resonance for relativistic particles.
